Where to go from here? Seeking journalism advice

Be careful not to burn yourself out.

You become a better writer by experiencing, not necessarily just churning out writing forever constantly. If you can, travel. If not, do some weird jobs. Get outside of your comfort zone. (It will help you become a better journalist by learning how to interact with people, since that's 90 percent of journalism.) Using those experiences, you widen your perspective — that can help you find angles, sources, and story ideas that you may never have thought of before.

Once you've done that, you can start a blog to write about those experiences, but the thing is everyone who's coming into/going out of journalism school has a blog. The pressure's going up to have actual clips in publications. It shows you're hungry, and — honestly — I'm so glad my early college work wasn't published online immediately due to editing errors and writing style.

But I have to be frank: in order for you to pursue a career in writing, you can't focus on the awards. Some of the best journalists I know were average students in university. It's about your passion for the career, the hunger you have to continue onward and keep pushing.

A mistake I see in a lot of recent journalism grads is that they're naive. They think that by keeping their nose to the ground and doing work, they become a better journalist. You become a formulaic journalist, not necessarily a good one. You can practice the inverted pyramid all day, but that's not going to make you a passionate writer.

If you're planning to do journalism, double major in journalism as well as the foreign language you'd like. Most publications want a bachelor's in journalism or a related major. Plus, you'll get a lot of valuable information. It is very hard to get into journalism now without a bachelor's degree. It can happen, but it's very difficult.
